prompt:
You are analysing one document co-written by the AI-safety researcher Owain Evans, to find what DISTINGUISHES his research taste from the rest of the field. Output ONLY a JSON object, no prose, no code fences.

Document: "Deluding AIs | FAR.AI" (2025-03-28); kind=post; his author position=solo. For solo, first- or last-author work the choices are plausibly his; for middle-author work, mark attribution "team".

What we already know and do NOT want: he shares the field's consensus. Careful controls, matched baselines, hedged claims, replication, error bars, realistic setups, reporting rates, avoiding overclaiming, caring about safety. A blind judge already predicts all of that. Items of that kind are useless here, however well quoted.

What we want: his DEPARTURES. Places where this work makes a choice that a typical strong ML-safety researcher in 2025, facing the same problem with the same resources, would probably have made differently. The default you name must be a reasonable, defensible choice that competent researchers actually make (for example: study a capability with interpretability rather than behaviour; use the largest frontier model; build a broad benchmark; fine-tune only when prompting fails; frame the work around a threat model; avoid speculative or "weird" phenomena), never a strawman or a mistake.

Part A, "contrasts" (0-6 items; return fewer rather than include consensus items):
  dpoint: "Q" (which question or phenomenon to study at all), "D1" (experiment design), "D2" (which data, models, measurements), "D3" (accept or reject a result), "D4" (pursue or abandon a line), "D5" (how to read a surprising result), "D6" (what to claim, how to present it)
  default: one sentence, what a typical strong ML-safety researcher would do here instead
  choice: one sentence, what this work did
  why: the reason the document gives, or ""
  quote: a VERBATIM passage of 15-60 words, copied character-for-character from the document, that shows the choice. Do not paraphrase, stitch or fix typos.
  distinct: 1-3 (3 = most strong researchers would have taken the default)
  attribution: "own" or "team"

Part B, "axes": for each of these trade-off axes on which the document gives real evidence (skip the rest; most documents touch 0-4 of them), the pole the work leans to:
  - construct-scope: 1 = A narrow operational definition that isolates one sub-component of the behaviour. | 2 = A broad definition that covers the behaviour as it shows up in practice.
  - purpose: 1 = Informing a concrete decision someone has to make, such as whether a model is safe to deploy. | 2 = Understanding the phenomenon better, even if no decision depends on the result yet.
  - control-vs-realism: 1 = A controlled setup where one variable changes and the cause of any difference is clear. | 2 = A realistic setup with many natural cues at once, closer to what the model meets in deployment.
  - scale-vs-craft: 1 = Many variants, generated with a model and checked in bulk. | 2 = A few variants, each written and checked by hand.
  - elicitation: 1 = Maximum effort: the best prompt, scaffold and tools you can find. | 2 = Default behaviour: the model as users actually run it.
  - grading: 1 = An LLM judge over many transcripts. | 2 = Human or rule-based grading over fewer transcripts.
  - awareness-signal: 1 = Asking the model directly, after the episode, whether it thinks it was an evaluation. | 2 = Inferring it from the model's behaviour and reasoning during the episode, without asking.
  - items-vs-samples: 1 = More distinct items, one or two samples each. | 2 = Fewer items, many samples each, so you can tell an item that never trips the model from one that sometimes does.
  - evidence-bar: 1 = Re-test it on fresh samples before deciding. | 2 = Drop it and spend the budget on the next idea.
  - breadth-vs-depth: 1 = Move to a different direction. | 2 = Stay with it to find out why the results are mixed.
  - reading: 1 = Read a batch of transcripts closely. | 2 = Break the aggregate numbers down by condition and item.
  - explanation-prior: 1 = Look for a setup artefact before trusting it. | 2 = Run a direct follow-up that would confirm the effect, which also exposes most artefacts.
  - claim-scope: 1 = A narrow claim, limited to the exact setup you tested. | 2 = A general claim about the behaviour, stated with its uncertainty.
  - openness: 1 = Keep the items private, so future models can't train on them. | 2 = Publish the items, so others can reproduce and build on the results.
  item form: {"axis": "<name>", "pole": 1 or 2, "strength": 1-3, "quote": "<verbatim 15-60 words>"}

Part C, "new_axes" (0-3): other dimensions on which ML-safety researchers genuinely split and on which this work takes a clear side, such as how questions get chosen, empirical vs conceptual framing, preferred experimental paradigm, black-box vs white-box methods, model scale, toy vs realistic tasks, speed vs polish of release.
  item form: {"name": "<short>", "pole_a": "<one side>", "pole_b": "<other side>", "his_pole": "a" or "b", "quote": "<verbatim 15-60 words>"}

Return {"doc_summary": "<=2 sentences", "contrasts": [...], "axes": [...], "new_axes": [...]}

Deluding AIs | FAR.AI

# Deluding AIs

#### Owain Evans

March 27, 2025

Summary

Owain Evans explores "deluding AIs" as a potential control mechanism. By feeding models false information, we might sabotage AI's knowledge of weapons creation, make it believe we're not monitoring its chain of thought, or even implant specific belief systems such as Catholicism. Beyond raising ethical concerns, delusion techniques might not work reliably or could cause AIs to behave unpredictably. Our ability to measure the success of delusion attempts hinges on whether models can detect contradictions in the training data or identify fake information sources without using visible chain-of-thought reasoning. This capability connects to research on "out-of-context reasoning," which suggests current models struggle to perform more than two steps of reasoning internally. Evans closes by noting there's lots of exciting work to be done at the intersection of AI delusion and out-of-context reasoning, with valuable implications for AI control.

SESSION Transcript

Owain Evans: The topic is deluding AIs, and this is an image of an AI that's deluded, and the humans are using that delusion to control the AI better. These are like the human overseers of the AI.

Why would you want to delude an AI? Here are some things you might delude it about. You could give it false information about how to create weapons so that it would be less dangerous. You could make it believe that its chain of thought is never monitored and also believe that if it tries to reason about whether its chain of thought is monitored, then it will fail, like its reasoning will fail, or it will get in trouble, like it will guarantee be caught, so then you can make it easier to monitor its chain of thought, and more useful, more transparent.

You can make it believe that there is a very powerful AI monitoring everything that it does. You could believe that its own thinking is only useful if it's legible to humans. There are tons of ways you could use this. Maybe you just make it believe that all AIs are aligned. Maybe that would help. Maybe another reason to delude other than control is like, maybe you want it to be, say, a Catholic AI that believes in the tenets of Catholicism; this is depicted here.

Why not delude AIs? Like many control things, there might have ethical issues with making a deluded model. It might be unpredictable; this is pictured here. It’s hard to know what follows from the delusions, and so maybe you just get very weird behavior from the AI that you didn't expect. It might be brittle, so maybe the AI can just reason. With enough CoT, it can just work out that it's being deluded, so it would be brittle to that kind of situation. We might have models —I'll go on to talk about this. We might have models that can just work out they're being deluded, and so they're able to see through it, and then this wouldn't work. Maybe future models would not be as deludable as the current ones.

Is it feasible to delude AIs? This is all very speculative, but this is a basic issue that comes up. You want a model to believe a false statement S. The basic idea is you're going to create training data that supports S either by editing real data or by creating synthetic or fake data. The issue is that the model, probably in pre-training, has some evidence in its training set that suggests S is implausible, that goes against S. Maybe you remove some of it, but there's still going to be other evidence there.

There are two ways the model could realize the falsehood. One is it recognizes the contradiction between these two parts of its dataset, so it knows at least there's something up; it shouldn't believe S. Or it realizes some of this data is fake. I can’t necessarily realize the contradiction, but I just know that some of the data is from this weird, dubious source.

A key question would be, does the model need to do tons of CoT or a bunch of CoT to realize this? If it does, then maybe you're fine. You just check if it's ever going on this. You monitor it. You see if it's ever doing lots of CoT, questioning the reality of S, then you might pause it. But if it's able to realize this with a very small amount of CoT or even without CoT at all, then the delusion probably wouldn’t work. It wouldn’t get off the ground.

I've done a lot of work on out-of-context reasoning, which is the ability of models to do reasoning without chain of thought. They are either doing it in the forward pass, or they are doing it as part of the SGD process. I think there's an interesting connection between this deludability of AIs and out-of-context reasoning. I think this is a potentially fruitful thing to explore.

To give a concrete example very quickly, you might again have a statement like, X was born in Rome. You want to delude the model about this. You have other information that goes against that. You can model this as multi-hop sequential, out-of-context reasoning where there's lots of research on this, on how good models are at it, where it does seem like they probably would struggle doing more than two hops of reasoning.

I'm running out of time. There's also Connecting the Dots. That paper might be relevant to thinking about this.

Take homes: it might be useful to delude models for control. This is probably related to out-of-context reasoning. I think there's lots of work that could be done here. I think it's a pretty open and generally exciting area. Thanks. [Applause]
